PAPER: Archival Science (2026) 26:1 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10502-025-09522-9 ORIGINAL PAPER A child, a passion, and a mission to fill the gap: Affective, social, and personal impacts of a German minority community archive Magdalena Wiśniewska‑Drewniak1 · Adriana Kapała1,2 · Agnieszka Rosa1 · Kamila Siuda1 Received: 15 July 2025 / Accepted: 13 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract This article, based on empirical data, especially interviews conducted in August 2024, examines an independent community archive that currently operates in south- western Poland, in the region of Silesia. The German Minority Research Center’s main goal is to preserve German identity and language among Germans in Poland, to study and document the community history and popularize their input in the his- tory of the region. The article focuses on social, affective, and personal impacts of the German Minority Research Center’s archive. Analysis indicates that the archive preserves endangered heritage, supports cultural initiatives, empowers women, and addresses minority issues like German identity. It builds trust within the minority community and helps create counter-narratives. Data also indicate the lack of trust of the German minority in Polish state (public) archives. Archival contributors expe- rience both stress and satisfaction, gaining skills and career opportunities. However, sustainability and the emotional demands of archival work remain challenges. The article argues that independent archives like GMRC provide scholarly and commu- nity value, offering alternatives to mainstream institutions and fostering personal and collective reflection. Keywords Community archives · Independent archives · Archives impact · German minority · Minorities in Poland Introduction Community archives are gaining increasing interest from scholars, archival profes- sionals, and heritage institutions (Poole 2020, p 658; Wiśniewska-Drewniak 2020, pp 357, 362). While definitions vary, in general, community archives are grassroots initiatives, with some level of independence, created to preserve traces of an event, social group, or physical location that, according to the archives’ creators, have been Extended author information available on the last page of the article Vol.:(0123456789) 1 Page 2 of 24 Archival Science (2026) 26:1 inadequately or erroneously documented and represented in public heritage institu- tions. Many authors also stress community engagement in this process (Welland and Cossham 2019; Poole 2020). Community archives are well documented in Anglo- phone literature, and interest in grassroots archives is growing globally (Flinn et al. 2022). Poland is a notable example of recent development in this area. The Center of Community Archives in Warsaw (Polish: Centrum Archiwistyki Społecznej, hereafter: CCA), a cultural institution aimed at promoting and helping grassroots archives, lists over 840 Polish community archives, mainly focused on local history (Center of Community Archives 2025). Despite the fact that Poland is rather a homogenous, not very diverse society (over 98% Polish, nearly 90% Catho- lic according to 2021 census data; Statistics Poland 2023), there is also a number of minority-based community archives that document groups such as Roma, Jews, Lemkos, Armenians, and Germans. One example, described in this article, is the German Minority Research Center (Polish: Centrum Badań Mniejszości Niemieck- iej, German: Forschungzentrum der Deutschen Minderheit, hereafter: GMRC) which preserves the history and life of the German minority in Poland. This research is part of the ‘Impact of Independent Community Archives’ pro- ject (hereafter: The IMPACT Project), which examines the social and emotional effects of three Polish community archives. The project, planned for implementa- tion in 2023–2026, is being carried out at the Faculty of History, Nicolaus Coperni- cus University in Toruń, Poland. This article, describing one of the three case stud- ies planned in the project, focuses on the GMRC archive and, for context, briefly reviews the post-1945 history of Germans in Poland. Methodology and sources The main data source was qualitative interviews with GMRC staff, collaborators, donors, and users (some respondents combined these roles) carried out in August 2024. In the second stage, four researchers used a priori codes (produced in the first phase of the project, based on literature, previous interviews with Polish community archivists and expert interviews) to analyze the archive’s impact, iteratively coding interviews and refining codes to capture both expected and new social and affective effects (UCLA Community Archives Lab 2018, pp 12–17). The initial set comprised 32 emotion-related codes, 58 codes concerning social impact, and 27 codes reflecting personal impact. In analyzing the GMRC data, some codes were merged or renamed, and additional previously unrecognized codes were introduced to the list: disappointment, ‘community archive sucks you in’, dreams, 1 Page 4 of 24 Archival Science (2026) 26:1 curiosity/interest, delicacy/sensitivity, mysticism, affect as a selection criterion (affective impacts); archive as a spokesperson for the community, family, commu- nity need for an archive, (legal) recognition of minorities, showing multicultural- ism (social impacts); repaying a debt, opportunity to visit different places, personal reflection (personal impacts). This article presents only the most frequent codes and the most significant impacts relevant to this community archive, omitting less com- mon findings in order to maintain a coherent narrative. However, all codes/impacts will contribute to the study in its final stage, aimed at cross-case analysis based on data from three community archives. The researchers first coded the interviews individually before moving to joint readings during meetings, where they compared codes, negotiated meanings, and developed a shared language to describe archival impacts. Individual coding enriched the process by revealing diverse perspectives shaped by different research experiences, understandings of community archives, and sensitivities. Collabora- tive engagement further broadened the analysis by capturing contexts that a single researcher might overlook. Joint discussions also enabled real-time resolution of uncertainties and the construction of an ontology, particularly when attempting to linguistically frame very subtle indications of impact, often expressed as: “I sense an influence/emotion here, but cannot name it.” Such an analytical strategy proved val- uable in studying elusive and intangible aspects, such as emotions and non-material influences. Archives and their impact Research on the impact of community archives stems from earlier analyses of librar- ies and public archives, where economic and quantitative studies dominated (Der- fert-Wolf 2018; Murzyn-Kupisz 2018; Poll 2018). One of the first projects to assess the impact of archives was Archival Metrics (2005–2011), which analyzed, among other things, the economic impact and effectiveness of online tools, indicating that archives attract researchers and tourists (Yakel et al. 2012). Studies also point to the educational importance of archives (Duff and Cherry 2008; Krause 2010; Daniels and Yakel 2013). Studies on the impact of community archives are few and far between and mainly focus on the UK and the US. An example is the Community Archives Develop- ment Group study (UK, 2006–2007), which found that community archives support skills development and lifelong learning, social integration and a sense of belonging (Community Archives Development Group 2007; Flinn 2010, p 154). In the US, Caswell et al. analyzed the impact of the South Asian American Digital Archive (SAADA), indicating a sense of ‘representational belonging’ among members of this community (Caswell et al. 2016). Gabiola et al. (2022) drew attention to the risk of retraumatization that community-based archives may carry and the need to protect the right to be forgotten. However, the context of these US- and UK-based studies might not always be applicable to other locations. To date, no research has been conducted in Poland on the impact of archives, although the topic has been discussed theoretically, especially in the context of their social role and relationship Archival Science (2026) 26:1 Page 5 of 24 1 with people (the so-called anthropologization of archivistics; Magier 2009; Jabłońska 2019; Rosa 2019; Chorążyczewski 2020). The IMPACT Project uses a simplified understanding of impact as ‘a noticea- ble or observable change in something’ (UCLA Community Archives Lab 2018, p 16), also taking into account the diverse nature of that change (positive or negative, intentional or unintentional, short- or long-term, critical or trivial; Brophy 2005, p 44). Duff and Caswell (2020) list four types of archive impact: educational, eco- nomic, social, and affective. The IMPACT project focuses on social and affective influence. We understand affective impact broadly, as ‘a culturally, socially and historically constructed category that both encompasses and reaches beyond feelings and emo- tions’ (Cifor 2016, p 10). This means that the affective impact we perceive includes, for example, joy, fear, catharsis, trauma, sensitivity, curiosity, and aspirations. Social impact is the impact of archives on their immediate community and those outside that community. It can be related to, for example, addressing social exclu- sion, impact on health, community safety, employment and education, developing personal and collective identity, expanding understanding of history (Wavel et al. 2002, pp 6, 19–20), stronger and safer communities, health and well-being, and strengthening public life (Horton and Spence 2006, pp 49–50) or development of skills and attitudes in volunteers, preservation of histories not found elsewhere, pro- motion of community and local pride, empowerment, and revitalizing endangered traditions (Duff and Caswell 2020, pp 56–57). Initially focused on social and affective impact, the project later added personal influence—direct effects on individuals, such as career, education, and personal growth. The analysis also considered possible negative impacts, not just positive ones, according to recommendations from the scholarly literature (Gabiola et al. 2022) and some expert interviews (interviews with Caswell, Flinn and Ogass Bilbao in: Wiśniewska-Drewniak 2025c). Germans in Poland after 1945 After World War II, Poland underwent major political and territorial changes: it became a communist state under Soviet influence, lost eastern lands to the USSR, and gained western and northern territories from Germany. Most Germans in these areas fled or were displaced in accordance with the provisions of interna- tional agreements, as Poland was intended to become a nationally homogeneous state (Madajczyk 2001, pp 18–19; Czok 2023, pp 26–27). The years after World War II remain sensitive in Polish–German relations due to the expulsion, disposses- sion, and discrimination of Germans, as well as their detention in specially created camps (Madajczyk 2001, pp 24–38, 106–109, 118–121; Kaszuba 2007, pp 493–499; Berlińska and Madajczyk 2008, pp 238–252, 273–290; Matelski 2016, pp 41–43). The Silesia region, where the GMRC operates, is characterized by mixed identities and languages (Polish, German and Silesian; Czok 2023, pp 93–97), and it suffered greatly in 1945 from violence by the Red Army (Kaszuba 2007, pp 471–480). As part of the so-called ‘Recovered Territories’ (portrayed by Communist propaganda 1 Page 6 of 24 Archival Science (2026) 26:1 as having always been Polish; Berlińska and Madajczyk 2008, pp 217–219), it was re-populated by Poles mainly from Central Poland and displaced persons from the Eastern Lands lost to the USSR (Kaszuba 2007, pp 486–493). According to the official narrative by the communist state, there were no more Germans in Poland after the displacement action ended, and the minority was not officially recognized. The years 1945–1990 were a period of systemic elimination of German heritage and so-called (re)Polonization (‘de-Germanization’) in the Western and Northern Territories, which the Silesian language and identity also fell victim to (Kaszuba 2007, pp 509–510; Gołasz 2016; Świder 2016; Czok 2023, pp 26–28). This period of several decades was internally diverse (Browarek 2016), but in gen- eral, for the German minority, it meant discrimination, inability to use and teach the language and a lack of freedom to associate (Madajczyk 2001, pp 127–128, 148–149, 154–158), and research on German history was either frowned upon or strictly controlled (Czok 2023, p 30). In 1980s, unsuccessful attempts were made to register German minority organizations (Madajczyk 2001, pp 321–327). That became possible only after the democratization of the country in 1989/1990 (Honka 2016, pp 92–93). According to the 2021 census, German national-ethnic identification was declared by more than 144,000 people (including 42,500 as the first and 23,500 as the only one) and German is spoken at home by more than 216,000 people. The largest number of people with German identification and language live in the Opol- skie voivodeship, where GMRC is located (Statistics Poland 2023). Although there is no systemic discrimination today, tensions sometimes arise between Poles and the German minority, especially over the public use of the German language and differ- ing views on history (Czok 2023, p 118). German Minority Research Center and its archive The GMRC is an association of NGOs working for the German minority in Poland. It focuses on organizing research on Germans in Poland and documenting the his- tory of this minority, especially the formation of minority organizations since 1980s. The Center is headquartered in Opole, and its activities mainly cover Opole Sile- sia, but also Northern and Western Poland, where the German minority is the most numerous. The Center preserves German identity and language in Poland, promotes intercultural dialogue, corrects misconceptions about Germans, and encourages young researchers to study minorities, especially the German minority in Poland. The origins of the Center are linked to the 1991 Polish–German Treaty of Good Neighborship and Friendly Cooperation, which guaranteed the rights of the Ger- man minority in Poland to preserve and develop its identity, use its language freely, establish cultural and educational institutions, and practice its religion (Republic of Poland 1991). In 2010–2011, the German-Polish Round Table reviewed the imple- mentation of the Treaty and committed Poland to establishing a research unit on the history and heritage of the German minority (German-Polish Round Table 2011, p 1), but no such institution was established for several years. In 2015, the House for Polish-German Cooperation (a non-governmental organization located in Polish Archival Science (2026) 26:1 Page 7 of 24 1 Gliwice) took matters into its own hands, launching the documentation project “Ger- man Minority Research Center”. The Center began its independent operations in 2020. The GMRC’s collections document the history of German minority organizations in Poland and, to some extent, the history of Germans in Poland after 1945. The col- lections include interviews with representatives of the German minority (including founders of minority organizations); private archives of activists (individuals active locally as well as representatives of the German minority in the Polish Parliament); documentation of German minority NGOs, often of a very local nature; German- language press and publications; and a small number of museum objects (GMRC on zbioryspoleczne.pl 2025). The archive contains about 500 oral history recordings, about 48 running meters of shelves, more than 450 GB of data (more than 22,000 files) (as of October 2024). The GMRC conducts research and publishes materials on Germans in Poland, organizes meetings, discussions, and conferences, collaborates with universities and research centers, and compiles a biographical dictionary and bibliography of the German minority. While it does not organize its own exhibitions, it lends objects to the permanent exhibition ‘Germans in Poland—history and present’ at the Doc- umentation and Exhibition Center of Germans in Poland (part of the local public library). GMRC representatives visit local German minority groups to present the archive’s work and support records management in these organizations, aggregate information about local groups and their records, and showcase the Center’s collec- tions and activities to students and visitors. GMRC finances its activities mainly from grants from the German Ministry of the Interior, through the Union of German Associations, and also uses Polish funding, such as from the Department of Religious Denominations and National Minorities of the Ministry of the Interior and Administration, also awarded on a competitive basis. A small percentage of the budget comprises local grants and membership fees. GMRC employs several staff on project-based contracts (full-time or part-time), so jobs lack stability. In addition, external individuals work with the Center, and the archive is supported by interns and volunteers. The head of the archive, Ewa Czec- zor, leads daily archival work (including contacting donors and collecting materials, digitizing collections, describing materials and providing access) and was the main study participant and the bridge between the researcher and other respondents. At the same time, Ewa made it clear that she really wanted to take part in the study ‘to leave her mark in the very end’. The conversation’s emotional intensity prompted the PI to include GMRC in the study. Ewa is a well-known member of the German minority, a former local journalist, well versed in the history and landscape of the German minority in Poland and well- known in the community, with experience in leading a local group of the Socio- Cultural Society of Germans in Opole Silesia (a German Friendship Circle, Ger- man: Deutsche Freundschaftskreise, DFK). At GMRC, she started by interviewing community members and later became head of the archive, focusing on commu- nity contacts and collecting new materials. She also collaborated with the Center of Community Archives in Warsaw, attending training sessions, congresses, and testing the Open System for Archiving (OSA)—a software administered by the Center of Community Archives, used by community archives to store and publish metadata describing collections, as well as to publish digital materials online. Ewa’s openness and commitment were crucial to the study’s success. Despite the emotional difficulty of leaving her beloved job, her self-reflection and willingness to participate enriched the study. Ewa actively supported the organization of the visit to Opole, introducing the PI to the local community and helping with logistics. This shows the importance of the relationship between the researcher and the person introducing them to the community under study, and the consequences of choosing this person for the course of the research. Social impact The GMRC is a young community archive focused on German minority research and works mainly with scholars rather than the broader community. It prioritizes collecting materials over outreach, resulting in limited social impact. Due to sen- sitive data, access is restricted and promotion is limited (Wiese 2024). Still, the authors note the archive influences its environment in various ways. Research value The GMRC archive is a unique and valuable resource documenting the history and present of Germans in Poland—a subject no other Polish institution covers. Its col- lections include archives from numerous German organizations (with more than 70 hyper-local groups), private archives of activists and politicians, interviews, and materials on wartime, post-war, and underground activities of the German minor- ity. GMRC also initiates research, especially in under-studied areas, and encourages young scholars. The archive uncovers unknown local histories and new perspectives, with oral histories adding emotional depth to the narratives about the past, allowing community members to find themselves and their families in those stories (Mazurk- iewicz 2024). Its materials are valuable not only to historians but also to political scientists, linguists, sociologists, and musicologists. Interestingly, both donors inter- viewed highlighted the archive’s research value and scientific potential as key rea- sons for contributing (Galla 2024; Paisdzior 2024). Archival Science (2026) 26:1 Page 9 of 24 1 Community needs GMRC is increasingly recognized by the German minority in Opole Silesia and beyond. By collecting physical materials, it addresses the need for a ‘central’ archive of the German minority in Poland, though some groups resist this centralization. Recently, many German minority organizations in Poland have transferred their old- est, unused documentation to the GMRC. As organization members age, preserving heritage becomes harder, and many groups will close, requiring their collections to be secured (Czeczor 2024b). The closure of local German minority circles (DFKs) has already led to scattered documentation and difficult access, highlighting the need for the GMRC’s centralized archive (Galla 2024). The center is the place where not only organizations, but also individual minor- ity members can deposit their personal archives and memorabilia. In this context, Ewa quoted one of the donors who said that ‘it would hurt his heart if they were to put it [the medal] in his coffin, so he would rather donate it to us’ (Czeczor 2024a). GMRC makes it possible to preserve personal mementos of community members, a point also made by donors Ryszard and Helmut. The latter stated: Do I know if my grandchildren or great-grandchildren will be interested in this? They’ll put it in the furnace or in a bin and it just will be gone. I abso- lutely do not know. I, for one, always hoped that something like this [like GMRC] would be created, and so many years it waited, and finally it was born (Paisdzior 2024). Saving endangered heritage Another impact of the GMRC is rescuing the heritage of Germans in Poland that is often not only scattered but also at risk of destruction. This rescue mission is high- lighted in interviews, like Michał’s account: ‘a colleague who went to this interview pulled two, three binders from him [the donor] with his documentation […], as they were already standing by the stove. It was a matter of days’ (Matheja 2024). Ewa stated that archive rescue operations were a top priority during her tenure, though often done ad hoc and in haste in liquidated German minority organizations (Czeczor 2024a). Center members learn about endangered heritage through commu- nity contacts, media monitoring, cooperation with German organizations and donor families, and by responding to individual reports. Valuable examples of materials rescued by the GMRC are the Kroll’s lists (lists of people of German origin) from the late 1980s, likely the only surviving copies, unique records from local German minority groups and memories of the last com- munity members who recall the post-war era, communism, and the origins of Ger- man minority organizations—stories no one else is preserving. Impact related to the minority focus of the archive This group of meanings emerged from several influences that together form an ‘umbrella impact’ important because of the archive’s connection to the minority. 1 Page 10 of 24 Archival Science (2026) 26:1 These impacts are: little-known/marginalized stories (filling the gap) and building counter-narratives; nurturing identity and preserving language; ‘it’s more compli- cated’; showing Poland’s multiculturalism; dialogue between communities; recogni- tion of minorities; mainstreaming. One of the Center’s main goals, like many other community archives, is to fill gaps in the collections and narratives of public institutions (Flinn 2007, p 154, 160; Flinn 2010, pp 151, 158; Flinn 2012, p 32; Wakimoto 2012, pp 94, 119; Caswell 2014, pp 30–32, 36; Welland 2015, p 38; Caswell et al. 2016, pp 68–69). GMRC reveals the complex identity and history of Opole Silesia and the history of Germans in Poland—poorly known and marginalized by the communist state: When I started looking into this, I posed the question, what is the history of the German minority in Poland, when did [it] begin? [...] It’s not like we came here to Poland en masse and created a minority in [19]90. Our history is deeper, only we were not recognized before, but just because we weren’t rec- ognized doesn’t mean we didn’t exist (Matheja 2024). Weronika sees a role for the GMRC in, among other things, filling the gaps in the narrative about the history of Germans in Poland caused by the state’s failure to recognize this minority: I think that in terms of documenting history, some kind of continuity, it is really invaluable that there is such an archive, especially in the context of the fact that for 45 years [between 1945 and 1990] the minority was not officially recognized and had no opportunity anywhere else to record this history of theirs. This is now a restoration of sorts, and it is very tedious work (Wiese 2024). She also turns to personal, family experience, comparing the opportunities of her generation and two generations back: And I know, my grandparents didn’t have this opportunity, they couldn’t speak German, they couldn’t pass on the language, they couldn’t talk about their his- tory, their experiences, and all this we have now here and we can show it. It’s still way too late, but at least at this point it’s happening (Wiese 2024). GMRC also seeks to correct erroneous narratives about the past of Germans in Poland by creating its own counter-narratives: ‘we are showing and securing evi- dence that this hitherto written story about the origins of the German minority is not fully reflected in the documents’ (Czeczor 2024a). Fostering identity is a common impact of community archives discussed in the literature (Flinn 2007, pp 159, 162; Flinn 2010, pp 154, 161; Flinn 2011, p 11; Flinn 2012, p 31; Caswell 2014, p 35; Caswell et al. 2016, pp 73–75). This is especially important for minorities, who continually face assimilation and integration pres- sures. Preservation of the German identity and language is cited as a primary moti- vation for GMRC: So, we, of course, simply want to survive as a minority, and therefore any action that causes people’s knowledge of this minority, of its history, of its her- Archival Science (2026) 26:1 Page 11 of 24 1 itage to increase is important. This is something that is the foundation, actu- ally. Without knowledge, more than one generation cannot survive (Matheja 2024). Preserving German identity relies on maintaining the German language, which was banned in Opole Silesia during communism—impacting two interviewees. Michał calls his generation ‘lost in this respect,’ while Ryszard describes a ‘stigma,’ yet both continued the mission to save German identity and language started by ear- lier activists: My German is not perfect, I make mistakes, it’s natural, because I’m exactly the post-war generation that was at the ban not only on learning the language, but on using it at all. So here this stigma was heavily imprinted, but we also did not give up. Today, those ancestors of ours, who in the eighties, nineties... Some of them took constant care to preserve the language, the culture, because it had to survive in some way. And today we are carrying this legacy to the next generation. This is difficult, however, because each successive generation is different, so you have to work hard at it. But this is probably the case in every minority. There are no two ways about it, you have to fight (Galla 2024). An interesting impact is what the authors called ‘it’s more complicated.’ This describes how the community archive deepens and complicates the narrative of a social group—here, Germans in Poland—often seen as monolithic by the majority, despite internal diversity and ambiguous identity (Flinn 2010, p 154; Flinn 2011, p 10; Caswell et al. 2016, pp 71, 74). The GMRC highlights Poland’s multiculturalism, documenting both the his- torical and modern presence of Germans in the country, which was emphasized by Ryszard, advisor to the Speaker of the Sejm on national and ethnic minorities: ‘I think we should never say that we are a monolith. This is what they tried to teach us during the communist era. Besides, here the German minority has experienced it very much’ (Galla 2024). The same interviewee also sees the potential of com- munity archives for other minorities not officially recognized by the state, as these archives, by documenting a community’s past and contemporary presence in Poland, can contribute to its legal recognition (Galla 2024). GMRC also seeks to enter into dialogue with other minority communities and declares it is open to such contacts (Matheja 2024). The center brings knowledge of the German minority into the mainstream—on the one hand, it makes it visible outside the German community in Poland, and on the other, it also encourages people outside the community to participate in, for example, German minority research. GMRC does not claim exclusive rights to it: ‘We do not have a sole license to study ourselves’ (Wiese 2024). Competition in the heritage market An important role of community archives is to create alternative opportunities for donors who may choose to donate their materials to diverse types of entities. With their presence, community archives significantly diversify the ‘heritage market’ in 1 Page 12 of 24 Archival Science (2026) 26:1 Poland. It is significant that the GMRC collects materials from the German minor- ity, which had bad experiences with the Polish state in the post-war period. Since state archives are governmental offices, Polish Germans may have trust issues with them (more on trust below). Such claims appeared in interviews with Ewa (Czeczor 2024a) and Helmut (Paisdzior 2024). In turn, Ryszard expressed doubt that the state archives would be interested in this type of material at all (Galla 2024). Community archive as a partner Each community archive operates in its own complex ecosystem of collaborations and partnerships (Wiśniewska-Drewniak 2019, pp 163, 197–198, 243, 311, 386, 430, 482–483, 543). The main partner of the GMRC is the Documentation and Exhibition Center of Germans in Poland (part of the Voivodeship Public Library in Opole); an important group of partners is also organizations of Germans in Poland (in Opole Silesia and other regions) and dealing with issues of Polish-German rela- tions (e.g., the House for Polish-German Cooperation). The center also collaborates with numerous scientific institutions and the Center of Community Archives. GMRC thus interacts with local and non-local networks by being a partner (or potential partner) for cooperation for various state, local government, and non-governmental entities. To a limited extent, however, the center has established links with public, mainstream heritage institutions, such as local museums and archives. Empowering women A notable theme is the GMRC’s potential to empower women, especially through efforts to highlight their role in German minority organizations and share the sto- ries of German women in Poland. Ewa intentionally focused interviews on wom- en’s often-overlooked contributions, discussing topics like social welfare, hospi- tals, childbirth, cultural and humanitarian activities, work with children, dancing, singing, and women’s workplace challenges (Czeczor 2024a, 2024b). On the other hand, working at the GMRC enabled Ewa to re-enter the workforce after raising children, in part due to the availability of part-time positions. This support for flex- ible employment can be seen as empowering women by helping them return to pro- fessional life. Affective impact Trust and distrust Trust and distrust were common themes among interviewees. Those co-creating the archive (Michał, Ewa, Weronika) emphasize how important the trust of donors and the community is to them, and how they are influenced by the fact that they come from the community. Ewa emphasized the role of donors’ trust in the GMRC, which stems, among other things, from the ‘institutional’ underpinning of the Center’s Archival Science (2026) 26:1 Page 13 of 24 1 activities (which is a relatively stable NGO, connected with similar entities), the close ties with the German minority, and the fact that the Center is not a state insti- tution in which community members may have limited trust: because when someone comes from outside, people don’t want to donate, there’s this trust in these circles, that we have this support of these institu- tions [German minority organizations], and it’s not that we want to give it to the state archive. [...] It’s just that I know that these people, if they wanted to, would go to this state archive themselves. And they never did. Because this is a different story (Czeczor 2024b). Ewa emphasized the importance of trust when recording oral histories, particu- larly with difficult or traumatic memories, especially for women. She noted that such deep trust from interviewees can be challenging: ‘Sometimes you think it’s over- whelming that this person has given you so much trust,’ she says (Czeczor 2024b). Weronika emphasized that trust is crucial in the Center’s relationships with minority organizations, relying on both their location and personal connections with GMRC representatives—factors also important for recruiting oral history interview participants (Wiese 2024). Concern/anxiety A common theme in the analysis was concern and affective states like anxiety, fear, uncertainty, and loss of control. Donors often distrust state archives and worry about the fate of materials at GMRC, though trust in the Center helps ease this. GMRC staff also worry about the archive’s future, as, like in many community archives run by NGOs, its sustainability is threatened by reliance on project-based funding and annual grant competitions. Even getting funding in a given year does not mean immediate comfort, as funds are in fact paid out late. When, in one year, the pay- ments got delayed till August, the center was ‘pushed to the wall’ (Matheja 2024). As the head of the Center stressed: ‘when it comes to financial security, we tread a very thin line’ (Matheja 2024). Ewa sometimes worried her archival work, especially structuring the archive, was not good enough due to her lack of formal training and the complexity of German minority organizations. She sought advice from CCA and others (including during the interview, from the PI), but even after years of leading the archive, she still had doubts—feelings she described as ‘minority stress,’ involving ongoing responsibility and worry about the archive’s fate (Czeczor 2024b). Similarly, Weronika expressed doubts about what to scan during limited visits to minority organizations, often feel- ing rushed and unsure about her decisions (Wiese 2024). Trauma An important effect associated with GMRC is trauma, which is primarily due to the difficult fate of Germans in Poland in recent decades. Difficult topics are present in many of the materials collected in the GMRC archive: 1 Page 14 of 24 Archival Science (2026) 26:1 they felt German and also had a lot of problems after 1945, which was almost a natural thing in Poland. The social consent was that, after all, it was neces- sary to take revenge on these Germans, even though they were children at that point [during the war]. And these various difficult issues, they appear time and time again in documents and in interviews with people (Czeczor 2024a). These difficult topics include, for example, the experience (especially of women and children) of the Red Army’s advance into Silesia in 1945, forced migration and camps for Germans after World War II, discrimination during the communist period, difficulties in establishing German minority structures in 1980s, and women’s diffi- cult experiences in the workplace and family life. Sometimes, the traumatic experiences of members of the German minority are the reason why potential interviewees or donors choose not to share their stories with the center (Czeczor 2024b). The traumatizing content of interviews can also have a negative impact on those recording the interviews, causing them discomfort and mental strain (see ‘Personal impact’ for more detail). The archival ‘toil’ We coded ‘toil’ for feelings that archival work is tiring, time-consuming, heavy, monotonous, aggravating, and overwhelming. Ewa described processing materials as a ‘heap of work’ requiring many hours, saying she focused on emergency salvag- ing and lacked “passion and love” for archiving. She compared sitting in an archive to living in the cave of St. Jerome, the patron saint of translators and archivists (both her professions; Czeczor 2024a). She prefers meeting people and collecting mate- rials over the tedious task of arranging and describing documents, which is made harder by constant new arrivals and ongoing digitization. She often mentioned a lack of time, unfinished work, and necessary compromises. Weronika also recalled collecting materials for GMRC as absorbing, exhausting, time-consuming, and tedi- ous (Wiese 2024). A sense of mission and satisfaction GMRC creators feel a strong sense of mission, believing their work is valuable and benefits the community: ‘I had the feeling of such a mission, that I wanted to save it somewhere, but I also belonged to this community.’ Weronika spoke of honoring previous generations by sharing their untold stories and giving them voice (Wiese 2024). Ewa described their efforts as ‘doing our job’—preserving culture and fulfill- ing an inner need through the community archive: ‘We are doing our job. We are saving culture; we are extending something that is simply in us, because it is simply in us; it cannot be denied’. She also spoke about the realization of her inner need through the community archive (Czeczor 2024a). Even when the center’s team arrives too late to collect some materials, Ewa focuses on the positives—they still manage to preserve many other stories: Archival Science (2026) 26:1 Page 15 of 24 1 This is [...] the most common answer, that these people are no longer alive. Well, yes, but we still saved so much and so many of these interviews. So it’s positive, it’s always an added value, because otherwise we’re always too late, for many questions [...] (Czeczor 2024b). Helmut and Ryszard, both donors and founders of the Center, also emphasize the mission to preserve the heritage of Polish-German for future generations. Ryszard sees the GMRC’s work as continuing the efforts of German minority activists since 1980s. (Galla 2024; Paisdzior 2024). Ewa repeatedly expressed satisfaction with her work for the GMRC, especially from the materials she collected. This sense of fulfillment is tied to her situation during the interviews, as she was about to leave the center and reflecting on her con- tributions to the archive: I’m very happy that I’ve been able to co-create this over these last few years here and secure a part of the region’s history, and that’s a very, very positive thing for me. This gave me the greatest satisfaction: getting to know these peo- ple. And the fact that I’m going [away] for a while or forever, it remains to be seen, but I’ve left my mark here and it makes me so happy, but also sad (Czec- zor 2024b). Passion and enthusiasm Ewa says she approaches her GMRC work ‘with great passion,’ especially enjoying collecting materials and interacting with people over typical archival tasks (Czeczor 2024b). She also values collaborating with CCA, where she met other enthusias- tic community archivists who, like her, prioritize personal connections over simply accumulating archival materials: ‘And that’s what I also like about these people, that they are so passionate’ (Czeczor 2024b). Joy and pleasure The analysis shows GMRC as an archive that brings joy and pleasant feelings. A highlight of the PI’s visit was watching 1990s chronicles with Ewa—colorful, photo- filled records made by children at German minority summer camps. Ewa fondly noted, ‘People used to make such chronicles, no one makes them now…’ (Czeczor 2024b). Showing the chronicle, Ewa came across a familiar face: Oh, no, Anetka [...], that’s too much! […] She’s on my Facebook, she will be happy. I have to take a picture of it [the chronicle]. And that’s so cool, isn’t it? […] Oh, my! About Anetka, I laughed out loud at this point. […] Well, and sometimes that’s what’s cool—that you open [a document] and say, ah, gee, I knew that one (Czeczor 2024b). This accidental encounter shows how valuable and affectively charged the doc- uments in the community archive can be—especially for a person with direct and close ties to the community that the archive documents. 1 Page 16 of 24 Archival Science (2026) 26:1 Ewa shared a story about a fortunate event that brought someone great joy. Although she usually didn’t accept newspapers, she once took in Opole periodicals from the Hitler era. Just three days later, the German Consulate in Opole requested newspapers from a specific date for a senior citizen who was looking for newspa- pers published on her birthday. To everyone’s delight, GMRC had the exact copy: ‘I made a scan and someone was happy, God, thanks […]!’ (Czeczor 2024b). Ewa also mentioned a donor from Germany, who was very happy and emotional to donate several hundred photographs to the center from a liquidated organization (Czeczor 2024b). Certainly, the emotions associated with the transfer of materials to the com- munity archive are a very interesting issue that requires further study and are only hinted at here. Personal impact Personal impacts are the direct effects of a community archive on individuals, espe- cially community archivists. These include ‘hard’ impacts (like career growth) and educational impacts (gaining new skills), as well as ‘soft’ impacts (personal devel- opment, not related to career development). As a subsidized NGO with paid staff, GMRC offers specialists’ jobs and profes- sional growth. For example, Ewa returned to work after raising children and was inspired to pursue formal archival education; she eventually had to resign for fam- ily reasons, but she completed the Association of Polish Archivists’ registry course (Czeczor 2024a). This shows community archives can motivate formal education in archival studies. Similarly, Weronika’s work at GMRC led her to take up her doc- toral dissertation on the German minority in Upper Silesia in 1981–1991 and shaped her career within German minority organizations (Wiese 2024). Working at the GMRC offers opportunities to learn new skills, such as record- ing oral history interviews, digitizing materials, and using OSA. Archivists develop competencies through self-study, practice, and CCA trainings. Key skills gained include oral history interviewing, archival expertise, and digital proficiency. Over time, they become experts in both archive management and the collections’ subject matter, which in this case is the history and contemporary organization of Germans in Poland. ‘Soft’ personal impacts are less tangible and varied. For Ewa, working at the center was a way to give back to the German minority that enabled her bilingual education (Czeczor 2024b). The experience deepened her awareness of Silesian and German minority history, social change, digitization, and people’s responses to hardship. The archive made her reflect on her role in history, appreciate the present, and see her own identity in the past but also reflect on the uncertainty of the future. Ewa also managed to notice the loss of identity in the German minority in Poland and perceive some aspects of history differently (Czeczor 2024a, 2024b). Weron- ika said co-creating the GMRC helped her discover herself and define her direc- tion (Wiese 2024). Archival work also shifted attitudes—Ewa became more criti- cal of German minority activists (Czeczor 2024a) and valued cultural work more (Czeczor 2024b). Interviewees felt that they could make a positive difference for the Archival Science (2026) 26:1 Page 17 of 24 1 community, realize themselves, create good memories, meet new people, and visit new places through GMRC. While positive impacts dominate the interviews, some negatives also appear. Ewa found it hard to distance herself from the many difficult stories included in oral his- tory interviews and sometimes felt overwhelmed by interviewees’ trust (Czeczor 2024b). Similarly, Weronika stopped recording interviews for GMRC because she found it mentally and emotionally exhausting: I was too emotional, and after each interview I would sit for half an hour and cry in the car, because something there moved, moved me, and I thought that it was too much sometimes. [...] the thing that moved me a lot was that I couldn’t keep my distance (Wiese 2024). We did not collect data from oral history interviewees, but Ewa believes discuss- ing past traumas can be therapeutic, as witnesses often share these experiences for the first time (Czeczor 2024a, 2024b). However, while oral history interviews may be healing, they also risk the retraumatization of witnesses, making it a complex issue (Gałęziowski & Urbanek 2017; Gałęziowski et al. 2018; Vickers 2019; Mason 2024). Discussion and conclusion The study confirms some impacts of community archives previously identified in the literature, pointing among other things to their research potential, which, although not crucial for the narrative about community archives, has been recognized before (for example, Flinn 2007, p 160; Flinn 2012, p 32; Caswell 2014, p 30; Caswell et al. 2016, p 68; Bacia 2020, pp 30–35, 38; Chorążyczewski 2015, p 22; Wiśniewska- Drewniak 2019, passim) and was mentioned by some experts interviewed in the previous phase of the project (interviews with Ogass Bilbao, Płuciennik, Stefanac, Więch, and Ziętal in: Wiśniewska-Drewniak 2025c). Interestingly, the data show that donors were strongly motivated by the archive’s research potential. The analysis also confirms the role of community archives in rescuing endan- gered heritage. The studied archive preserves the at-risk cultural heritage of the German minority, often excluded from official heritage institutions. This rationale aligns with a widespread motivation among community archives and is reflected in the prevalent Polish discourse on the subject, which frequently employs expressions such as ‘saving from oblivion’ or ‘saving endangered heritage/history/past/tradition.’ The data also indicate a correspondence between the impacts and motivations of GMRC and those described in the literature on community-based/community-led archives from, for example, the US (Caswell 2014; Caswell et al. 2016) and the UK (Flinn 2011). Though in a very different location and context, the studied archive documents the history of a minority group, including experiences of discrimination and marginalization, creates counter-narratives to official versions of history, and fills in narrative gaps from the perspective of minority members. As with similar initiatives in other parts of the globe, the archive seeks to strengthen group identity and language, complicate the narrative about a given group, and promote the group 1 Page 18 of 24 Archival Science (2026) 26:1 and its history among the rest of the population. In Poland, minority archives play an important role in highlighting the country’s multiculturalism, educating about both historical and present-day coexistence among various groups, promoting toler- ance, countering discrimination, and challenging stereotypes. However, their actual impact in this regard remains difficult to measure and calls for further research. The research confirmed the previously described educational potential of com- munity archives (Community Archives Development Group 2007; Jura Consultants 2009, p 17; Wakimoto 2012, p 100; Lian and Oliver 2018, p 326), helping archivists gain new skills, such as digital, archival, and oral history interview skills. The inter- views, however, also made it possible to identify effects that had not been previ- ously described in detail in the literature, and which we provisionally refer to as ’soft personal impacts’. Data show that engagement in a community archive can foster personal growth by encouraging reflection and changing perceptions of history and a community, deepening one’s self-awareness and self-esteem (due to feeling useful), changing one’s attitudes, or allowing for self-fulfillment. Yet, the archive’s personal impact has mostly been studied in relation to its creators, with much less known about its effect on users. This disparity arises because users who are not affiliated with community archives are typically more difficult to engage, and at GMRC, the majority of users are also associates, thereby constraining the range of accessible data. Yet, the authors recognize this to be an important area for future research. The study also points to other emerging interactions and contexts of commu- nity archives. Among them is their role as a ‘central archive’ (in this case: of the German minority in Poland), serving community members and numerous minority NGOs as a shared space, where they can deposit their documentation and memora- bilia. This phenomenon is particularly notable considering the strongly emphasized role of trust, both within the community and toward the community archive itself (stemming from the archivists’ belonging to the community), alongside a simul- taneous lack of trust toward public archives (which, in turn, legitimizes the need for an archive created by and for the community). The case of GMRC also shows how community archives provide an alternative for potential donors, creating a kind of competition within the heritage sector, which now becomes an “open market,” where no one has a monopoly to accept donations from private individuals. Moreover, community archives have changed the Polish heritage landscape, com- plementing this ecosystem and becoming a potential partner for other institutions and organizations. Like GMRC, they mainly form local networks, interacting with like-minded organizations, schools, libraries or local governments, but rarely with public museums and archives (Wiśniewska-Drewniak 2019, pp 580–581; Melon 2023, pp 41–42). It has not been adequately described before and certainly requires further analyses of the interaction networks of community archives; however, this study indicates that community archives are becoming another significant compo- nent of the ecosystem of cultural and heritage entities. The study shows that community archives such as GMRC evoke deep posi- tive emotions and can bring joy and pleasure, make people smile, and evoke good memories. Participants also experience a strong sense of duty, fostering lasting commitment. This shared mission can also motivate donors to contrib- ute to these archives. These observations align with how Polish narratives about Archival Science (2026) 26:1 Page 19 of 24 1 community archives describe passion and enthusiasm as the emotional forces driving archivists’ commitment (Bewicz et al. 2021; Wiśniewska-Drewniak 2018, pp 72, 76; Ziętal 2018, pp 293, 295). Yet, while research often highlights the positive impacts of community archives (with the notable exception of Gabiola et al. 2022), our analysis also found negative effects at GMRC, such as anxiety and self-doubt, as well as emotional burden and potential secondary trauma, especially related to oral history work. The issue of trauma in archives, though increasingly described by the scholarship worldwide (Laurent and Hart 2018; Sloan et al. 2019; Laurent and Wright 2023; Regehr et al. 2023; Sexton 2025), is still underrecognized in Poland, with only a few exceptions (Wiśniewska- Drewniak 2021, pp 188–189; Korpalski 2024) and should certainly become an important line of research in Polish archival studies—not only in the context of community archives. This case study demonstrates that it is possible to successfully apply a new view of archival value: considering the positive emotional impact of materials beyond just their scientific or informational worth (Caswell 2020, p 153). The presented narrative on GMRC’s impact, supported by contextual information about Germans in Poland, can inform future research on community archives. The study and the detailed archive description in the case report offer valuable comparative material for examining similar initiatives, such as other German minority archives, archives of other minorities in the region, archives serving as regional networks, or central hubs collecting materials from multiple NGOs. Comparisons can also be made with archives significantly differing from GMRC—for example, those of heavily dispersed or majority communities, fully digital projects, or collections dominated by either very traumatic or solely positive materials. Such analysis can reveal vary- ing strategies for building trust, engaging communities, and addressing emotional outcomes. The article’s discussion of social and affective effects may also guide future researchers by providing initial analytical categories for further empirical refinement. A final project publication will share (in an open data repository) a com- prehensive list of impacts identified across three case studies, offering a reference framework for future qualitative and quantitative research on community archives. JSON: Name: community_archive_impact_pipeline Title: A mixed-methods longitudinal impact evaluation pipeline to quantify the social, affective, and personal effects of community archives on volunteers, donors, and users Short Hypothesis: Active engagement in a community archive causes a measurable increase in archival competency and perceived community belonging among volunteers within six months compared with matched non-participating community members. Related Work: Existing work on archive impact has produced descriptive case studies and localized evaluations that document skills development, identity formation, and research value in community archives, with several projects producing qualitative taxonomies of impacts and small-scale quantitative measures. Prior comparative efforts are limited, geographically concentrated in Anglo-American settings, and often focus on positive outcomes (skills, learning, representational belonging) without standardized, reproducible measurement instruments. Major shortcomings are (1) the lack of validated, cross-case metrics for affective and social outcomes; (2) limited longitudinal or causal inference designs that distinguish pre-existing differences from effects of participation; (3) scarce empirical attention to potential negative impacts, such as secondary trauma and chronic workload stress for archivists; (4) under-sampling of non-affiliated users and donors, producing selection bias; and (5) absence of a shared open dataset and codebook that supports replication and cross-context comparison. These gaps constrain generalization and prevent reliable assessments of trade-offs (e.g., empowerment vs. emotional cost). Abstract: There is currently no standardized, empirically validated pipeline to measure whether and how community archives produce social, affective, and personal impacts for the people who create, contribute to, and use them. We propose a mixed-methods longitudinal evaluation pipeline that combines (1) a validated survey instrument for archival competency, perceived community belonging, and well-being; (2) a reproducible qualitative coding taxonomy for affective and social themes; and (3) archival operational metrics (donation rates, digitization throughput, access events). The pipeline is designed for multi-site deployment and causal testing using matched control groups and mixed-effects models. The main contribution is an open, replicable methodology and reference dataset that enable quantification of both positive (skills, belonging) and negative (anxiety, secondary trauma, sustainability stress) impacts over time. Expected outcomes include statistically estimable effect sizes for participation-driven change, an interoperable codebook for affective/social archival impacts, and empirical evidence to inform archive practices and future comparative research. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Primary sites: three community archives (including GMRC) with heterogeneous subject focus; (2) participant cohorts per site: volunteers/staff (N=60), regular donors (N=60), regular users (N=60); matched non-participant community controls per site (N=180) sampled by propensity score matching on age, education, prior civic engagement; (3) archival operational logs and donation inventories for 24 months pre- and 24 months post-intervention. Data types: baseline and follow-up surveys at T0, T1 (6 months), T2 (12 months) including standardized scales: archival competency (custom scale, 8 items), perceived community belonging (Likert, 6 items), subjective well-being (WHO-5), secondary trauma symptom checklist (10 items), and trust-in-institutions scale (6 items); semi-structured oral-history interview transcripts (recorded, transcribed); digitization and accession logs. Baselines: matched controls and historical pre-engagement operational metrics. Evaluation metrics: primary outcomes—change in archival competency score (mean difference, Cohen's d), change in perceived belonging (mean difference, Cohen's d); secondary outcomes—change in well-being and trauma scores, donor retention rate, accession rate, access-event rate. Statistical tests and models: paired t-tests for within-subject pre-post changes; mixed-effects linear regression with random intercepts for site and subject to estimate treatment effect of participation, controlling for covariates; propensity score matched difference-in-differences estimator comparing participants to matched controls; mediation analysis testing trust as mediator between participation and donation behavior; multiple comparison correction via Benjamini-Hochberg. Qualitative analysis: apply a predefined codebook (derived from IMPACT taxonomy) with inter-rater reliability assessment (Cohen's kappa target >=0.7); thematic saturation checks and NVivo/Atlas.ti coding logs. Ablation and comparisons: (A) Ablation 1 — exclude oral-history activities from the engagement protocol to measure differential trauma outcomes; (B) Ablation 2 — compare centralized-deposit model versus in-situ local retention model across matched local groups to measure donor trust and preservation rates; (C) Coding ablation — compare results using full taxonomy versus reduced (skills-only) coding to quantify loss of affective signal. Power and sample assumptions: target minimum detectable medium effect (d=0.5) with 80% power at alpha=0.05, accounting for clustering by site; anticipated attrition rates modeled at 20% by T2. Data release: de-identified survey data, codebook, and annotated transcripts deposited in an open repository. Risk Factors and Limitations: Recruitment and selection bias due to volunteer self-selection into archival roles; social desirability bias in self-reported measures; small number of sites limits external validity beyond the studied regional and minority contexts; language and cultural differences across sites complicate instrument equivalence and comparability; longitudinal attrition reducing power at T2; ethical risk of retraumatization for interviewees and archivists; limited ability to randomize assignment to participation (necessitating quasi-experimental matching with residual confounding); variability in archive operational practices reduces standardization of the intervention; incomplete or inconsistent archival logs constraining operational metrics; compute and staffing limits for large-scale qualitative coding; findings may not generalize to fully digital community archives or archives in markedly different socio-political environments; funding instability at community archives may change site behavior during study period and confound causal inference.
